BP Follows Shell in Exiting Indonesian Gas Station Retail as Local Partners Take Full Control
sum: JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — British energy giant BP Plc has agreed to divest its entire equity holding in its Indonesian fuel retail venture, following a similar retreat by peer Shell Plc in offloading local gas station networks to domestic operators.

Under the transaction disclosed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), BP is selling its 49.9% equity stake in PT Anugerah Parama Retail (APR)—the joint venture operating the BP-AKR service station network—to affiliates of local logistics and energy player PT AKR Corporindo Tbk (AKRA) for $14.22 million (approximately Rp 231 billion).
The buyout allows AKR Group to consolidate complete control over the retail operation, lifting its combined interest from 50.1% to 100%.

According to regulatory filings submitted to the bourse, AKR Corporindo affiliates Akrida and ADH jointly acquired 11,444,565 APR shares previously held by BP, representing 49.9% of the venture's issued and paid-up capital.

"Akrida and ADH jointly purchased 11,444,565 APR shares owned by BP, representing 49.9% of the issued and paid-up capital in APR, with a share purchase price of $14.221 million," AKR Corporindo Corporate Secretary Arum P Handayani stated in an official exchange disclosure.

The divestment aligns with BP’s broader global mandate to rationalize capital deployment and simplify its retail forecourt portfolio across selected emerging markets. AKR emphasized that the buyout will not disrupt ongoing business operations. "This transaction does not create any material negative impact on the operational activities, legal standing, financial condition, or business continuity of the company," Arum added, noting that the transaction did not trigger mandatory material or affiliated transaction thresholds under Financial Services Authority (OJK) regulations.

BP’s retreat from Indonesian forecourt ownership mirrors the recent corporate restructuring executed by Shell. In late October, Shell completed the transfer of its domestic retail gas station operations to local energy distributor SEFAS Group through PT Isla Energy Indonesia.

sum: BP has picked up fresh backing from two major Wall Street houses, with UBS and Wells Fargo both lifting their price targets on the same day the oil major completed the sale of a majority stake in its lubricants arm. The stock, however, refused to join the party: BP shares were down 2.0% in trading, a reminder that upgraded targets and a stronger balance sheet do not always translate into immediate buying interest.

The Castrol transaction, closed today, hands 65% of the lubricants business to Stonepeak and delivers BP net proceeds of $6 billion after tax. The company intends to direct that money toward debt reduction. BP keeps a 35% stake in the new joint venture and can sell the remainder after a two-year lock-up period. Stonepeak has named former Shell chief executive Ben van Beurden to chair the new Castrol board.

UBS analyst Joshua Stone raised his target to 725 pence from 700 pence while reiterating a buy rating. His case rests as much on operations as on the disposal proceeds: BP beat expectations for a third consecutive quarter in Q3, with adjusted net income running 15% above consensus. That distinction matters for valuation — an asset sale is a one-off cash injection, whereas quarterly results speak to ongoing earning power.

Wells Fargo, for its part, lifted its target to $63 from $57 and kept an overweight rating, arguing that debt reduction opens the door to higher shareholder returns in 2027. The bank pointed to operating cash flow of $14.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, excluding working capital movements, which came in ahead of its own $12.9 billion estimate.

Those numbers sit alongside the figures BP reported for the quarter: an adjusted replacement cost profit of $8.458 billion, against $2.210 billion in the same period a year earlier, operating cash flow of $14.8 billion, and net debt reduced to $13.9 billion. Reuters reported that BP has already hit its net debt target a year ahead of schedule, with the Castrol proceeds set to reinforce the balance sheet further.

Investors hoping the windfall will flow straight into buybacks or a richer dividend should temper expectations. BP is prioritising the available funds for debt reduction, and the company has made no commitment to extra share repurchases or a higher dividend.

In a trading update ahead of its October 30 earnings release, BP estimated that net debt declined to between $13.5 billion and $14.5 billion at the end of September, compared with $22.3 billion at the end of June. The reduction puts the company ahead of its previously announced debt reduction targets.

BP’s refining indicator margin increased to an estimated $46.70 per barrel during the third quarter, compared with $29.60 in the second quarter and $15.80 a year earlier. Stronger refining economics are expected to contribute an additional $1.9 billion to $2.1 billion in profit from the company’s products business compared with the previous quarter.

The improvement reflects tighter global refined product markets as geopolitical disruptions, including the conflict involving Iran, have affected petroleum supplies and international transportation routes.
BP also expects its natural gas marketing and trading performance to improve significantly from the second quarter, while oil trading results are projected to remain broadly unchanged.

The company estimated third-quarter upstream production between 2.19 million and 2.24 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, compared with approximately 2.20 million barrels per day in the preceding quarter.

Despite the stronger operating outlook, BP warned of additional impairment charges totaling between $3 billion and $4.5 billion, primarily associated with its gas and low-carbon energy businesses. The charges follow earlier write-downs involving renewable energy investments and reflect continued adjustments to the company’s asset portfolio.

sum: BP and Shell shares climbed on Wednesday as oil extended its rise amid a widening war between the United States and Iran.

Shares in BP (LSE:BP) and Shell (LSE:SHEL) rose again on Wednesday, extending a rally in UK oil majors as crude prices pushed higher on an escalating war between the United States and Iran. The move builds on gains made over the past two trading sessions.

BP shares are trading at 538.2p in late morning dealings on Wednesday, up 1.68% from Tuesday’s close of 529.3p. Shell shares are up 1.74% at 3,310.5p, having closed Tuesday at 3,254p. Both stocks remain below their highs for the year: BP peaked at 609.4p in March and Shell reached 3,758.5p in early June. Both are also well above last year’s lows of 393.3p for BP and roughly 2,554p for Shell.

Oil prices have risen as the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which began at the end of February, shows fresh signs of escalating. US forces completed an 11th consecutive night of air strikes on Iran late on Tuesday, and Brent crude was up as much as 4% on Wednesday, according to CNBC, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran was “not serious” about peace talks.

The conflict has also spread to shipping lanes. Yemen’s Houthi rebels declared what Reuters described as a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia this week, and two Saudi oil tankers reversed course in the Red Sea on Tuesday after Houthi threats, according to the Insurance Journal. Separately, Reuters reported that vessel crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, fell further on Tuesday amid lingering security concerns.

This is not the first time the war has driven BP and Shell shares higher. BP’s stock rallied as much as 28% after the conflict began before giving back about a fifth of that gain from its March peak, according to the Telegraph. Oil prices had briefly returned to pre-war levels in June after an interim US-Iran deal reopened the Strait of Hormuz, only for renewed disputes over the waterway to send energy costs spiking again.
Sentiment on the oil majors has turned more constructive since Shell’s second-quarter trading update earlier this month.

sum: The BP (LSE: BP) share price has given investors comfort at a tricky time. While many FTSE 100 stocks have been knocked by Iran war volatility, it’s a clear and obvious beneficiary. But for how much longer?

There have been ups and downs in recent weeks, depending on the prospects for peace. Yet overall, BP shares have done well. They’re up 16% in the last three months, and a stunning 53% over one year. Dividends are on top. Long-term BP investors might also say that it’s about time too.

Despite that strong run, the stock trades at roughly the same level as it did at the start of the millennium. It’s had a bumpy 25 years, plunging with the rest of the market after the 2001 dotcom crash, and taking further hits from the financial crisis in 2007, the Deepwater Horizon tragedy in 2010, and Covid lockdowns in 2020.

The Ukraine war drove up the oil price but also forced BP to take a massive £25bn hit on its stake in Russian state-owned oil company Rosneft. The group also battled with boardroom issues, which saw the last two CEOs, Bernard Looney and Murray Auchincloss, depart suddenly. It’s also struggled to respond to climate change pressures.

Q1 results (28 April) revealed a strong start to 2026, with quarterly revenue up £5.3bn to £52.3bn. BP’s trading division struck black gold, as customers raced to secure energy supplies. However, investors can’t assume this will continue. So much depends on what happens to Iran and the oil price.

BP’s bumper profits also attracted fresh attention from the Treasury. The current ‘windfall’ charge already accounts for around a third of the total taxes it pays to the UK government. Now Chancellor Rachel Reeves has scrapped a tax rule allowing oil and gas companies to offset UK profits against overseas losses, to fund a £1.8bn cost-of-living support package.

Today (25 May), there’s another issue to consider following reports that the US has struck a peace deal that would see Iran give up uranium and open the Strait of Hormuz. If the market wasn’t closed for a Bank Holiday, I’d imagine the FTSE 100 would be soaring, and BP shares would be heading the other way. Although you never know with these things.

This could accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels and towards home-grown renewables.

Also, the war is hitting infrastructure, and BP faces both longer shipping routes and higher operating costs. Its net debt was already a hefty $25.3bn in Q1. BP stock gains as Q2 2026 earnings beat estimates and oil prices surge
sum: BP p.l.c. (ISIN GB0007980591) stock is trading around 42.68 USD on the New York Stock Exchange as of August 31, 2026, after a session in which the price rose by 0.81 USD or 1.92 percent according to a recent options-linked quote snapshot compiled by MarketBeat on that date.

According to an earnings and options overview summarized by ad-hoc-news.de with data sourced from MarketBeat, BP reported earnings per share of 2.22 USD in Q2 2026, ahead of the 1.87 USD consensus estimate by 0.35 USD and delivering a positive surprise of about 18.7 percent in that quarter.

The same Q2 2026 data set indicates that BP generated revenue of 69.11 billion USD for the quarter against a consensus estimate of 57.89 billion USD, meaning revenue exceeded expectations by 11.22 billion USD and rose by 106.1 percent compared with the prior year quarter based on the cited analysis.

In addition to the strong top and bottom line beats, the Q2 2026 figures summarized in the MarketBeat based overview show that BP posted a net margin of 2.49 percent and a return on equity of 16.63 percent in the quarter, highlighting that the company converted the higher revenue environment into solid profitability metrics.

The broader energy backdrop has turned more favorable in early September 2026, with Brent crude prices approaching the mid 90 USD per barrel range and West Texas Intermediate moving into the low 90 USD zone amid renewed geopolitical tensions involving the United States and Iran in the Middle East.

As reported by The Business Times on September 2, 2026, Brent futures rose by 4.16 USD or 4.6 percent to settle at 94.65 USD per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate futures climbed by 4.46 USD or 5.2 percent to 90.22 USD per barrel in the latest completed session.

A separate crude price overview dated September 2, 2026 notes that Brent crude was recently quoted around 96.42 USD per barrel, up 1.77 percent on the day, while WTI stood near 91.77 USD per barrel with a gain of 1.72 percent, underscoring how supply risk premia have been rebuilt into the futures curve.

Shell and BP shares sink as China slams ‘bully’ US over oil dispute
sum: Shares in FTSE 100 oil giants took a tumble on Wednesday as President Donald Trump ramped up the pressure on Venezuela to hand over oil.

Shell had sunk near four per cent by midday to 2,644.7p whilst BP was down 3.5 per cent to 416.65p. The losses in the oil giants – which make up over £200bn of the blue-chip index’s market cap – weighed on the FTSE 100, dragging it to a 0.6 per cent slump and putting a firm end to the New Year rally.
It came as the price of brent crude – the international benchmark for oil – fell below the $60 mark to $59.97 after a 1.2 per cent slump.

“Record highs for the FTSE 100 and Dow yesterday came as the initial equity bounce reached a peak, but today’s focus is more on the slump in oil prices, which seem to be set for a new push to recent lows,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, told City AM.
Oil’s volatility followed Trump declaring Venezuela would be “turning over” $2bn worth of oil to the US – a move that would be set to impact trading relations with China.

The US’ Energy Information Administration estimates Venezuela has near 303bn barrels worth of crude – near 20 per cent of the world’s resource – but exports just 900,000 per day with China acting as the biggest customer.
Beijing has fiercely denounced the US’ actions, with a foreign ministry spokesperson accusing the US of “brazen use of force” and “typical acts of bullying”.

sum: The cheapest Brent crude price in five years today weighed on BP (LSE:BP.) and Shell (LSE:SHEL) as the oil majors joined Rolls-Royce Holdings (LSE:RR.) and BAE Systems (LSE:BA.) among the laggards of a weaker FTSE 100 index.
Share price movements in the energy and defence sectors were influenced by last night’s indication from Washington that a Russia-Ukraine peace deal has moved a step closer.
